meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I may be compelled to face danger, but never fear it'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Clara Barton everywhere, sourced nowhere. Absent from her published works, both standard biographies, and the famous 1862 letter you would check first.

answer.label: Not Clara Barton's documented words — an unsourced attribution
answer.authorDates: 1821–1912 · Civil War nurse & founder of the American Red Cross
answer.sourceLine: No letter, diary, speech, or book has ever been cited for this wording, and it appears in none of Clara Barton’s published works nor in either standard biography of her. The sentiment is authentically hers — she did write, in a documented 1862 letter, that she asked “neither pay nor praises, simply a soldier’s fare” — but this polished sentence traces back only to quote sites, not to Barton.

source.heading: The paper trail — and where it stops

docMeta.dd: None — no letter, diary, speech, or book has ever been cited
Barton's three published books; Epler (1915); W. E. Barton, 2 vols (1922)
The Life of Clara Barton, vol. 1 (1922), p. 159 — letter to Gov. John A. Andrew

source.excerpt: With this, my highest duties close, and I would fain be allowed to go and administer comfort to our brave men, who peril life and limb in defense of the priceless boon the fathers so dearly won. If I know my own heart, I have none but right motives. I ask neither pay nor praises, simply a soldier’s fare and the sanction of Your Excellency to go and do with my might, whatever my hands find to do.
trail: Barton’s own books do not contain the line. A full-text search of The Red Cross in Peace and War ↗ — roughly 250,000 words — returns nothing, and neither do A Story of the Red Cross or The Story of My Childhood.
Neither standard biography has it. William E. Barton’s two-volume life (1922) ↗, which reproduces her letters and diaries at length, and Percy Epler’s life (1915) ↗ both come back empty.

The nearest plausible candidate does not contain it either: the full text of her 12 December 1862 letter to cousin Vira ↗ — her famous letter from the eve of Fredericksburg, the one a reader would reach for first — has no such passage.
The curators leave it out. The Clara Barton Museum’s quotes page ↗ ties most quotations to a named letter and date — and this one is not on it.
source.cutTag: Letter to Gov. John A. Andrew, 20 Mar 1862
source.excerptNote: This is not the source of the popular quote — it is what Barton actually, documentably wrote about going to the front. Written from her dying father’s bedside in North Oxford, Massachusetts, and printed in William E. Barton’s biography, vol. 1, p. 159 ↗. Andrew replied within four days with a warm but conditional promise — which Dr. Hitchcock’s refusal then closed off.

sourceLink.text: Read the letter in The Life of Clara Barton, vol. 1 (1922)

source.rightsNote: Because the popular wording has no identifiable source, no copyright status can honestly be asserted for it — an unsourced line cannot be declared public domain. The documented Barton letter shown above is a different matter: it was published in William E. Barton’s The Life of Clara Barton (Houghton Mifflin, 1922), first published well before 1931, and is therefore public domain in the United States.

author.name: Clara Barton
author.heading: Clara Barton
author.metaLine: 1821–1912 · Civil War nurse & founder of the American Red Cross
author.bio: Clara Barton was a Massachusetts schoolteacher and patent clerk who, with no medical training and no official standing, talked her way to the front lines of the Civil War to carry supplies and nurse the wounded — earning the name Angel of the Battlefield. She later led the search for the missing dead at Andersonville, ran relief in the Franco-Prussian War, and in 1881 founded the American Red Cross, which she led until 1904. She wrote constantly — diaries, thousands of letters, and several books of her own — which is exactly why a sentence that appears in none of them deserves scrutiny.

cite.sourceCitation: No primary source has been located. The earliest traceable appearances are quote-aggregator listings — e.g. BrainyQuote, Internet Archive capture of 13 November 2019. For Barton's documented words on the same subject, see William E. Barton, The Life of Clara Barton, Founder of the American Red Cross, vol. 1 (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1922), 159.

misattribution.heading: How an unsourced line became a Clara Barton quote
misattribution.intro: Barton is a magnet name: a Civil War heroine whose real courage makes almost any brave-sounding sentence plausible. This one has been circulating for years, and every attempt to source it leads back to another quote page.

items.who: Her letter to cousin Vira, 12 December 1862
items.why: No carrier of the quote cites any source — but a reader who goes looking will land on Barton’s famous letter written at 2 a.m. before the Battle of Fredericksburg, held at the Library of Congress. It is the right register, the right year, and the most quoted thing she ever wrote, so it is the natural place to check. The full transcript ↗ settles it: neither “compelled to face danger” nor “never fear it” appears anywhere in it.

The quote was added on 19 April 2023 ↗ with a single footnote: a March 2021 post on the blog Historical Snapshots. That post ↗ quotes the line inside a narrative with only a general reading list at the foot — no citation for this sentence, and nothing in the list is offered as its source. The chain ends there.

BrainyQuote was already serving the line with no attribution beyond Barton’s name by November 2019 ↗. From there it spread to library and institutional blog posts, such as this one ↗, which repeat it without a date or source.
The wording appears in none of the books she wrote — not The Red Cross in Peace and War ↗ (some 250,000 words), nor A Story of the Red Cross, nor The Story of My Childhood.

misattribution.truthLine: What Barton verifiably wrote is better than the fake: from her father’s deathbed on 20 March 1862 she asked Governor John A. Andrew for “neither pay nor praises, simply a soldier’s fare and the sanction of Your Excellency to go and do with my might, whatever my hands find to do” — printed in William E. Barton’s The Life of Clara Barton, vol. 1 (1922), p. 159 ↗.

context.heading: Why this one is so easy to believe
lead: The line survives because it sounds exactly right. Barton really did go to the front with no rank, no pay, and no training; she really did stand in artillery fire at Antietam and Fredericksburg while surgeons worked; and she really did describe her own role as feeding and nursing men who could still fight. A quote that flatters an accurate reputation gets waved through without anyone asking where it came from.

But Barton is one of the best-documented Americans of her century. She kept diaries for decades, wrote thousands of letters, and published several books; her official biographer, William E. Barton, quoted her correspondence at extraordinary length across two volumes. When a “famous quote” from someone that thoroughly transcribed cannot be found anywhere in the record — and first surfaces on quote websites — the absence is itself the evidence.
detailsBody: On 20 March 1862, writing from her dying father’s bedside in North Oxford, Massachusetts, Barton asked Governor John A. Andrew for permission to go to the front: “I ask neither pay nor praises, simply a soldier’s fare and the sanction of Your Excellency to go and do with my might, whatever my hands find to do.” Andrew answered within four days.

That sentence carries the same meaning as the popular quote and has something the popular quote does not: a date, an addressee, a manuscript, and a printed page. The Clara Barton Museum’s own quotes page ↗ lists it — and, tellingly, does not list “I may be compelled to face danger.”
